item.title: How Dolly Parton turned self-aware artifice into authentic artistry
item.description: To be fake, to push into the sentimental performative aspects of the country genre, became her true autograph – a trace of her originality.
item.content:encoded:
Scrolling through the tributes to Dolly Parton this morning – from the Grand Ole Opry, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, queerfluencers and others – I thought to myself: that’s her real name?

Yes. The “Queen of Country”, who died overnight aged 80, was born Dolly Rebecca Parton. My surprise at the authenticity of her name says something about the contradiction within the figure of Dolly.

A sometime figure of ridicule and satire, the opening image of Dolly – in interviews, send ups and even her own branding – was often related to her apparent “fakeness”.

Her literal figure – breasts, face, hair – was obviously artificial. And often these synthetic additions to her body were transposed into an assumption she herself was, if not inauthentic, at least somewhat superficial. Dolly’s first hit on the country charts was Dumb Blonde in 1967.

But what a name! Not a diminutive of a serious name, not a stage name, but a real name that moves us towards her celebrity image as one: dressed-up, made-up, an object with which the entertainment industry played.

But the fact it is her true name pushes us into the performative savviness with which Dolly herself played. Her blondeness became a trademark, as did her pride and tongue-in-cheek irreverence for her “plastic” image.

item.title: Thriller: Kareem has outwitted death many times but he is not prepared for his dead wife’s return
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Relics of Love’, by Kashif Mashaikh.
item.content:encoded:
Discovering these artefacts, these relics of love, seemed to be an incomprehensible problem at first. I was sure that the fog would settle down, and Baba would guide me on a path to discovery. Digging up troubled graves, though, was a disastrous proposition. Some secrets, I believed, were best left untouched. But such virtues had been the core of her existence. She loved scraping a wound until it turned ripe and ulcerous so that she could cry and laugh at the same time, deriving pleasure from the self-inflicted pain.

“Where can I find these relics?” I asked Baba Sen.

“There are no maps. No flowcharts.” Baba smiled. “The journey leads to the destination. We ask the right questions. Look in the right places.”

One of Baba’s disciples, her head draped in a white pallu, walked in and handed over a black pouch to him. Baba held the sack in the flat of his palm and weighed it. Then he nodded his head and the disciple retreated as unassumingly as she had appeared.

item.title: ‘Implicated to satisfy public anger’: Ex-AAP leader moves HC against IB staffer murder conviction
item.description: On July 31, Tahir Hussain was sentenced to life imprisonment in the case.
item.content:encoded:
Former Aam Aadmi Party councillor Tahir Hussain has moved the Delhi High Court against his conviction for the murder of Intelligence Bureau staffer Ankit Sharma during the 2020 riots in the national capital, Bar and Bench reported on Wednesday.

On July 31, Hussain was sentenced to life imprisonment in the case.

Sharma was killed by a mob during the violence, and his body had been dumped in a drain.

In his appeal before the High Court, Hussain alleged that the investigation against him had been tainted from the start and was aimed at implicating him to satisfy public anger.

“Witnesses have been planted, statements of genuine eyewitnesses manipulated and the actual perpetrators have not been brought to book,” Bar and Bench quoted Hussain as saying in his appeal.

On July 13, a sessions court had convicted Hussain for murder, rioting, disobedience to an order promulgated by a public servant, promoting enmity between groups, rioting armed with a deadly weapon, unlawful assembly, and kidnapping or abducting with intent to secretly and wrongfully confine a person.

However, it cleared him of a criminal conspiracy charge.

In February 2020, violence broke out in northeast Delhi between supporters of the contentious Citizenship Amendment Act and those opposing it. The violence left 53 people dead and hundreds injured. Most of those killed were Muslims.

item.title: In Rajasthan, invasive tree helps tech giants buy carbon credits
item.description: Prosopis juliflora was planted to green the desert in Kachchh. Its biochar, now part of carbon offtake deals, is only helping more invasive trees grow.
item.content:encoded:
Decades ago, in the Banni grasslands of Kachchh, an invasive tree was planted to solve one environmental crisis. Today, big companies are paying to convert the same trees into a charcoal-like substance to solve another problem.

In January 2025, Google announced one of the largest biochar carbon removal deals to date, agreeing to purchase 1,00,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide removal credits from Varaha ClimateAg Private Limited, a Gurugram-based climate tech startup. Biochar is a carbon-rich charcoal produced by heating organic matter in low-oxygen conditions, which can store carbon in soil for hundreds of years.

By January 2026, Varaha had added Microsoft to its roster of corporate buyers, with Lufthansa, Swiss Re, and Capgemini also signing offtake agreements.

Among Varaha’s initiatives is a project in Kachchh, Gujarat, combining carbon sequestration with ecosystem restoration.

An invasive species

Prosopis juliflora was introduced to Kachchh around the 1960s to arrest desertification. The Banni grassland now has around 50% of its area dominated by this single invasive species, according to Khyati Thacker, a botanist who has spent over five years working on community-led ecosystem restoration in Kachchh and Saurashtra.

item.title: Lessons from Egypt: How the autocratic President Hosni Mubarak struggled with stability and growth
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Shortest History of Egypt’, by Maria Golia.
item.content:encoded:
Hosni Mubarak was a rectangular man, built low to the ground, boxy and taurine. When Egyptians nicknamed him la vache qui rit (“the laughing cow”), after a popular brand of cheese spread, it was derisive yet reminiscent of old titles like “great bull”, evoking a king’s virility. In his suit, tie and Ray-Ban aviators, with his lovely wife and sons, Mubarak was the image of a modern family man, but no ordinary one. The day when former president Anwar El-Sadat and 11 others died, Mubarak was close enough to be spattered with their blood yet he survived virtually unscathed. As president, he took no chances in keeping with the adage “trust in Allah, but tie your camel first”, never lifting the state of emergency declared after Sadat’s assassination, granting his security apparatus carte blanche under martial law to act on his behalf. As Egyptians bristled, he clung to the presidency past constitutional limits, feigning democracy with single-candidate referendums. He never appointed a vice-president and, towards the end, attempted to position his son as his successor.

item.title: ‘Malicious’: India rejects UN panel’s remarks about ‘targeting’ of Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslim
item.description: The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination had raised concerns about the ‘increase in law enforcement operations’ against the two communities.
item.content:encoded:
New Delhi on Wednesday rejected as “politically motivated” and “highly malicious” the United Nations’ racial discrimination watchdog’s observations about the alleged targeting of Rohingya refugees and Bengali-speaking Muslims by Indian law enforcement agencies.

On Tuesday, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination said that there had been an “increase in law enforcement operations targeting Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslims, migrants and asylum-seekers”, particularly following an order by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs in 2017 and the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack.

The 2017 order was an apparent reference to a directive issued by New Delhi that year detailing instructions for the deportation of undocumented migrants, including Rohingyas.

Weeks after the terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir’s Pahalgam in April 2025, the Union home ministry had directed the states and Union Territories to verify the credentials of persons suspected to be undocumented migrants from Bangladesh and Myanmar.

Following the May 2025 directive, the police in several states, most of them ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party, have been detaining Bengali-speaking persons – mostly Muslims – and asking them to prove that they are Indian citizens.

A student had approached the court seeking permission to wear a hijab with her school uniform after Tagore Public School in Prayagraj allegedly denied her admission to Class 11 because she wore a headscarf.

The High Court held that there was no material placed on record to establish that a Muslim woman or girl would be considered to have left the faith if she chose not to wear one.

The petitioner had argued that wearing a hijab was an essential religious practice protected under her fundamental rights to equality before the law and freedom of speech and expression.

She also said that she had been allowed to wear the headscarf at the same school from Class 6 onwards without objection.

In an order on August 21, the court said that the school might not have raised any objection in the past due to “lethargy, inaction, lack of will, non-enforcement of the uniform policy, even courtesy or hesitation”. item.title: ‘Toxic’ review: Blood, lust and something like love in unwieldy, overly long crime saga
item.description: Geetu Mohandas’s film, co-written by Yash and starring him in a double role, is out in cinemas.
item.content:encoded:
Toxic takes its “Adults only” certification very, very seriously. Geetu Mohandas’s latest movie, co-written with and led by Kannada star Yash, has genocide-level displays of violence interspersed with many examples of what is considered grown-up behaviour.

Yash, playing the gangster Raya, leaves no opportunity to grind, bash, slash and burn his way to power. This randy rando out-drinks the average alcoholic and puffs incessantly on cigarettes and cigars but still manages to keep his liver and lungs in good condition for whatever he sets his mind to.

Excess is the point in a 194-minute film that seeks to turn machismo on its head. On paper, Toxic threatens to re-examine the unreconstructed male character type personified by Yash in his KGF movies. Yash plays an anti-hero similar to Rocky from K.G.F but also different: Raya, unlikely Rocky, will be shown a mirror to the consequences of his actions, especially on the women he beds and sometimes weds.

Hyperbole will be used to cut hyperbole. Toxic will pile up the corpses, unleash the slo-mo swagger and roll out punchy dialogue, but there will be a larger, noble purpose to all of it – that’s the promise, at least.

Chauhan was the chief of defence staff during the military operation carried out against what India claimed were terrorist camps in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

The strikes were in response to the terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which killed 26 persons on April 22, 2025.

Speaking at an event in Delhi on Tuesday, Chauhan said that the Indian military did not launch munitions to deliberately target a nuclear site.

India had sent several munitions towards Sargodha to search for radars around the area, he said. “Kirana Hills is about 10 kilometres north of Sargodha,” added Chauhan.

The Donald Trump administration in the United States has paused immigrant visa appointments across the world, stating that consular officials had to be trained to screen out applicants who may need public assistance in the country, the Financial Times reported.

The US State Department has launched a global training initiative at all of the country’s embassies and consulates, an official was quoted as saying by the newspaper. Visa appointments would be adjusted to accommodate the training, he added.

Applicants who were slated for interviews at US embassies have received emails stating that their appointment would be rescheduled.

The training was aimed at helping officials identify applicants likely to become dependent on US public benefits, and at ensuring that visa applications are evaluated “comprehensively and consistently”, Reuters quoted the state department as saying.

The pause comes against the backdrop of the Trump administration seeking to tighten the rules for entry into the United States.

item.title: In Ladakh, an ancient art gallery is hiding in plain sight
item.description: Scattered across rugged boulders and exposed to the elements for millennia, Ladakh’s prehistoric petroglyphs reveal a deep history of trade and ritual.
item.content:encoded:
The phrase “open-air art exhibition” usually brings to mind a curated arrangement of contemporary artworks in elegant, manicured surroundings. But consider a different kind of public art display – scattered across rugged landscapes, exposed to the elements and unmoved for thousands of years.

In Ladakh, it is not unusual to stumble upon such a gallery in the wild, in the form of its vast and diverse heritage of ancient petroglyphs, or rock carvings. One such site lies at Alchi, 65 km west of Leh, within walking distance of its fabled medieval monastery. Access to the gated petroglyph field is easy by road and the site is officially open to visitors, though getting inside may require a little gymnastics to surmount the enclosure wall.

The exercise is worth it.

Atop a shelf overlooking the majestic downstream flow of the Indus lie about 250 large, smooth boulders bearing a gallery of primeval images. Strolling through the field, one spots animals, architectural forms, abstractions and inscriptions incised into the stone, their outlines stark against the dark obsidian lustre of the rocks. item.title: Why jobs are becoming unaffordable for some Indian women
item.description: Dalit or Muslim women often break barriers to secure formal employment, but struggle with the costs of living in a city while battling prejudice.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-three-year-old Ayesha* fought hard to study a master’s degree in social sciences and finally land a corporate job in Delhi in 2024. But within a year, she was struggling to stay afloat with her starting salary of Rs 40,000.

She was paying Rs 18,000 a month for a gated, paying guest accommodation, a metro-adjacent location and a neighbourhood she could come home to at night without planning ahead. After food, travel, groceries and sending money home, she was saving Rs 1,000 at best.

item.description: The coming election will serve as an important test of the political power of the billionaire class, and the broader health of American democracy.

In November, California will vote on a proposal to levy a one-off 5% tax on the wealth of all billionaires in the state.

Google co-founder and billionaire Sergey Brin has already spent US$100 million on political donations to a group opposing the tax. Brin is hoping to avoid a potential tax bill of US$13 billion, a return of roughly 130 to 1 if that investment is successful.

Advocates of the billionaire tax claim it would raise US$100 billion in revenue, to be allocated directly to state-funded healthcare, food assistance and public education.

item.title: A question of survival: Why Census 2027 must count Nomadic and Denotified Tribes separately

Census 2027 is crucial to the Nomadic and Denotified Tribes whose existence, culture, livelihood and identities are deeply connected to the fundamental right of being counted.

Community activists and leaders have repeatedly demanded that Nomadic and Denotified Tribes be counted separately in the Census. But these demands have been ignored even though the Census is much more than just counting people – it is fundamental to constitutional justice, policy-making and the equitable distribution of resources.

item.title: Living and longer and living well are not the same thing. Here’s why ‘healthspan’ matters more
item.description: The period of our lives we spend in good health is the goal we should be focusing on.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve spent more than three decades studying how exercise and diet keep us healthy. But one thing keeps showing up in the data: living longer and living well are not in sync. While we’ve partly solved the first one, we are lagging behind at the second.

Over the past century, the average Canadian’s life expectancy has increased by 22 years, to roughly 80 for men and 84 for women. Medical and scientific research may push those numbers higher. However, the number of years we can expect to live in good health has been declining, and in Canada it now stands at about 67, down from a peak of about 70 years.

That means a lot of us are on track to spend close to two decades, sometimes longer, living with chronic illness, cognitive decline or lost mobility. That gap, not lifespan itself, is the real crisis. And almost nobody treats it like one.

item.title: Online ornamental plant trade could be pathway for invasive species into India

item.content:encoded:
One of the world’s top 100 worst invasive species was brought to India in the 19th century as an ornamental garden plant. But Lantana camara, which now occupies 40% of India’s tiger habitats, was not the only one.

The ornamental horticulture industry is recognised as a key global pathway for introducing invasive alien species. A new study examining India’s online ornamental plant trade has found that a majority of these plants sold online are alien species, many of which are known to be invasive or naturalised in other countries.

The study, published in Environmental Conservation, also revealed that 57 species already declared invasive in India were available for purchase online, including Lantana camara and the highly-invasive Parthenium hysterophorus.

Invasive alien species are recognised as one of five major drivers of global biodiversity decline. “They outcompete our native species and the cost is enormous,” said Kesang Bhutia, the study’s lead author and a graduate student at Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), Bengaluru.

“Not all alien plants are a threat. There is a continuum,” explained Bhutia. A newly-introduced plant cannot survive without human care. Some escape cultivation, enter native ecosystems and naturalise, reproducing independently. Others can go further to become invasive.

item.description: The fire broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit around 3.15 am when a ventilator sparked, an official said.
item.content:encoded:
Three newborns died after a fire that broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit of a government hospital in Maharashtra’s Amravati district in the early hours of Monday, PTI reported.

The fire broke out at the Amravati District Women’s Hospital around 3.15 am when a ventilator in the unit sparked, the news agency quoted an unidentified official as saying.

Nine infants were in the room when the blaze began, The Indian Express reported. Hospital staffers evacuated all nine babies, but three of them died.

The remaining six babies have been admitted to a super speciality hospital.

Amravati Deputy Commissioner of Police Shyam Ghuge said that the fire was confined to one room in the neonatal intensive care unit and was doused within about 30 minutes, The Indian Express reported.

“There was a technical fault in the thermal unit, following which the fire broke out,” the official was quoted by the newspaper as saying. “The attendants immediately took out the nine babies from the room, of whom three died.”

item.title: Why has India-Japan cooperation not translated into deeper strategic integration?
item.description: Geography constrains operational reach, but deeper asymmetries, like threat perceptions, and economic vulnerabilities, define the scope of the partnership.
item.content:encoded:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s three-day visit to New Delhi in July 2026 for the India-Japan summit appears to have elevated relations between the two Asian countries into a fresh phase of strategic expansion. Ties had already undergone a remarkable transformation over the past decade, evolving from a largely economic and development partnership into one of Asia’s most consequential strategic relationships.

At its core, the logic of India-Japan convergence rests on a growing recognition that both countries have a stake in preserving a stable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific amid China’s expanding influence, safeguarding critical sea lanes, and strengthening economic resilience through diversified supply chains and trusted technology partnerships.

This convergence has produced tangible cooperation through defense dialogues, maritime exercises, and collaboration in areas such as semiconductors, critical technologies, and economic security. The defense understandings reached during the Takaichi visit, including progress on defense equipment and technology cooperation, reflect a growing focus on developing each other’s defense industries alongside strengthening military cooperation.

item.title: In clip, gangster Goldy Brar purportedly claims he killed Khalistan separatist Hardeep Nijjar

item.content:encoded:
Fugitive gangster Goldy Brar has, in an audio clip, purportedly claimed responsibility for the killing of Khalistani separatist leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada, The Indian Express reported.

The newspaper said it could not independently verify the authenticity of the audio clip, which was shared on social media.

Brar was purportedly speaking to Khalistan militant Paramjit Singh Pamma when he claimed that he and his associates killed Nijjar because he had allegedly been using young persons to sell drugs.

Brar, whose real name is Satinderjeet Singh, was heard saying in the clip that everyone “has to face the consequences of their actions”, The Indian Express reported.

“Those who groomed and incited 16-to-17-year-olds to sell drugs… those who blackmailed young people into selling drugs and becoming informants… Nijjar supported and strengthened these individuals so that he could use them when necessary,” Brar was quoted by the newspaper as saying in the audio recording.

item.title: Start the week with a film: How ‘Colony’ infuses fresh life into the zombie genre
item.description: South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho’s thriller can be rented from Prime Video and BookMyShow Stream.
item.content:encoded:
Few current filmmakers are having as much fun with the zombie genre as Yeon Sang-ho. The South Korean director of the brilliant Train to Busan and Peninsula has found inventive and intelligent ways to repeatedly unleash waves of the undead.

In Colony (2026), Yeon simplifies biotechnology and the concept of swarm intelligence to stage a hair-raising zombie attack in a shopping mall. Yeon uses every available element of consumerism, from advertising displays to mannequins, to explore the ways in which weaponised hive mentality can be combated by co-operation and trust.

The film can be rented from Prime Video and BookMyShow Stream.

The story begins with disgruntled scientist Young-chul (Koo Kyo-hwan) threatening to unleash a bioterror attack that only he can resolve. He isn’t joking, as the horrified people stuck in a shopping centre overrun by frothing, fast-moving zombies realise.

Se-jeong (Jun Ji-hyun) takes charge, using her academic credentials and understanding of ant colony dynamics to decipher how the zombies are evolving so rapidly and how they are so effective. Stuck with Se-jeong is a motley group that includes a security guard with a disabled sister and a bullied teenager. Yeon Sang-ho makes sure that these characters matter too.

item.title: How illnesses like smallpox in colonial India exposed Britain’s myths of control and invincibility
item.description: An excerpt from ‘In Sickness and In Death: How Faith, Medicine and Race Shaped British India’, by Ipshita Nath.
item.content:encoded:
As we know, the fear of contagion predominated most British reports of infectious diseases in India. The tropical climate of the subcontinent was blamed once again and the dangers of the “miasmatic emanation” were discussed frequently. As sanitary improvements were introduced under the colonial regime, reflecting the hygiene consciousness of the mid-19th century in Europe, the dread of the miasmatic towns of India intensified, leading to the increased focus on social class as a determinant of smallpox. In fact, poverty was discussed as a key element; it became an important factor in the epidemics. Consequently, the filthy habits of people, yet again, acquired prominence in the diagnosis and treatment of the disease.

Unfortunately for the British, while cholera and later plague were assigned to filthiness, smallpox did not particularly favour the black towns or the overcrowded chawls in the big cities. Once it struck, it quickly spread through the towns and villages alike, apparently without distinguishing between race and class. Still, administrative reports of the 19th century denounced the ignorant people of India for not being hygienic, and for dwelling in insanitary conditions, especially for living in “credulity and childish ignorance”. item.title: ‘Planned failure’: Is the Modi government sabotaging its own caste census?
item.description: Analysts, activists and politicians describe the chosen methodology for counting caste as a flawed one. Some even argue that the data will be useless.

“Most political parties recommended conducting a caste census,” the Cabinet had snidely noted in a press release then. “Despite this, the previous government opted for a survey instead of a caste census, known as the Socio-Economic and Caste Census.”

A year later, however, the Modi government has disclosed that it will follow the same method for counting caste that was used by Manmohan Singh’s administration. This has triggered allegations of sabotage, given that the data collected in 2011 was seen to be so faulty that it was never released.

item.title: Vitamin C can’t cure colds – how a Nobel Prize winner’s claims were disproved
item.description: Multiple studies conducted since Linus Pauling’s analysis showed that vitamin C has a minimal effect on colds.
item.content:encoded:
From the first hint of cold winter mornings, supermarkets and pharmacies begin heavy marketing to coax us to stock up on vitamin C to get through the cold and flu season.

But where did that idea come from?

As we’ll see, it’s a story including a Nobel Prize winner, a book and some claims that don’t quite stack up.

Nobel Prize winner writes a book

Linus Pauling was a chemist from the United States who won two Nobel Prizes. One was in 1954 for chemistry, for his research into chemical bonds. The other was in 1962 for peace, for his activism against nuclear weapons testing.

He was not a dietitian or an infectious disease physician. But that didn’t stop him publishing a book on vitamin C and colds in 1970. This book is widely credited with the skyrocketing sales of vitamin C at the time, a trend that continues today.

In this book, Pauling said we should consume high doses of vitamin C, around 1,000-2,000 milligrams a day for good health, and even more to prevent a cold.

His recommendations were said to be initially from one placebo-controlled trial in children on a ski camp in the Swiss Alps. He then analysed a further four studies conducted after his claims.

item.title: ‘Chakmak’: A poetry collection about tribal life is essential for the re-education of the urban mind
item.description: Poet Ramesh Karthik Nayak was awarded the 2024 Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar for these poems.
item.content:encoded:
Some time ago, I spent a week staying among and interacting with the staff and the students at three remote tribal schools of Dahanu Taluka in Maharashtra’s Palghar District. I stayed long enough to catch bursts of ebullience on the school playground day after day. That ebullience is the very force of nature running through their veins – the nature that they don’t see themselves as being distinct from.

Ramesh Karthik Nayak’s poetry collection Chakmak is replete with bursts of the very same ebullience throughout this book. It is best manifested in the way Nayak constructs his imagery. The abstract nouns or the qualitative adjectives that account for the lock, stock, and barrel of much of the imagery in mainstream poetry are not his weapons. Instead, it is the action verbs that convey the images in his poems. Consider the way Nayak captures nightlife in a forest:

Bats and owls
ransack the night.

He strips the image to the bare minimum and then lets the verb carry it. All the vividity and the vivacity of that image come from that one word: ransack. Even when an image is loaded with sensory words, it is his verbs that carry the image:

The ambience
of pollen dust-stained fireflies
churn darkness.

In September, 2015, Patrick Radden Keefe wrote about Ken Dornstein, whose older brother David had perished in Pan Am Flight 103 which had exploded mid-air, six miles above the earth. The debris fell over Lockerbie, Scotland. Over many decades, Ken kept trying to solve the murder mystery of his brother’s death. Who was responsible?

If a writer’s career is a sum of its parts, then all of Patrick Radden Keefe’s career has led to London Falling, his most recent non-fiction book. Ostensibly about the death of a teenager, Zac Brettler, in 2019, the book is a matryoshka doll of stories with charming rogues, liars, criminals and various nefarious types. item.title: After Maharashtra, Karnataka bans analogue paneer for one year
item.description: The order also applies to food business operators that use the non-dairy paneer as an ingredient.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration department has banned the manufacture and sale of analogue or non-dairy paneer marketed as paneer in the state for one year, the Hindustan Times reported.

Analogue paneer is a non-dairy or partially synthetic substitute for paneer. It replaces milk fat and milk solids with cheaper vegetable oils, making the dairy products cheaper.

A notification issued on August 17 prohibits the processing, packaging, storage, transportation, distribution and wholesale or retail sale of analogue paneer in the interest of public health.

The ban also applies to food business operators that use analogue paneer as an ingredient. Restaurants, food manufacturers, caterers and other food establishments have been prohibited from using, storing, supplying or selling such products in food preparation.

However, the notification does not cover standardised food products for which the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has prescribed separate quality standards. Products such as frozen desserts, processed cheese and mixed-fat spreads, which have their own recognised standards, are excluded from the ban.

The Food Safety Division said enforcement measures would be carried out across Karnataka to ensure compliance with the order.

On July 30, Maharashtra banned the production and sale of analogue paneer for one year, citing public health concerns.

item.title: Sunday book pick: The specific curse of dating men in ‘Nearly All the Men in Lagos Are Mad’
item.description: Published in 2021, this is Nigerian writer Damilare Kuku’s debut book.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria’s biggest city, Lagos, resembles a proper madhouse in Damilare Kuku’s 2021 debut book, the short story collection Nearly All the Men in Lagos Are Mad. It is hot and populous, and everyone’s hustling for more money or better sex. The men take shortcuts for both and women trip over themselves trying to make sense of this collective madness. Time and again they realise there is no substitute for extreme caution.

A heady romancescape

The 12 stories in the collection describe the experiences of cisgender women in various stages of heterosexual relationships. Women of all age groups and socio-economic classes suffer the madness of their men – but few take it lying down, finding ways to make the most out of their compromised circumstances. The title is catchy and relatable, and women in every city in the world will nod in approval. The men are a diverse set too, from cheating pastors to mama’s boys, from gay men to “alpha” Whites, men who endlessly pursue and those who are emotionally unavailable. Lagos’s heady romancescape often sweeps up unsuspecting women in its unique madness.

item.title: The 19th-century Indians who nurtured a self-reliant scientific culture in colonial India
item.description: The story of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science that helped an Indian win the Nobel Prize in Physics is a snapshot of these untiring efforts.
item.content:encoded:
One afternoon in 1907, a young accountant named Chandrasekhar Venkata Raman walked into the laboratory of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science at 210 Bowbazar Street in Calcutta.

Though he had a passion for the sciences, colonial India offered no stable careers in the field, so Raman had joined the Indian Finance Service.

But after work, Raman started a series of pathbreaking experiments – first in sound, then in optics – at the laboratory of the IACS, an institution that had been established just over three decades earlier specifically to popularise science and encourage Indians to conduct research at a time when such opportunities were scarce.

Soon, Raman (who would go on to become the secretary of the IACS) along with his associate KS Krishnan started experiments related to light. The phenomenon he recorded, where light changes its wavelength when scattered by molecules of a liquid, is called Raman Effect.

In 1930, this work earned Raman the Nobel Prize in Science, making him the first person from Asia to win this award.

item.title: 8.7 crore young Indians are ‘NEET’ – not in education, employment or training, says NITI Aayog
item.description: They need affordable or subsidised training and financial support, said the think tank in a report.
item.content:encoded:
An estimated 8.7 crore Indians aged 15 to 29 are not studying, working or undergoing training, said a report by the NITI Aayog, the main public policy think tank of the Union government.

The report, titled Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047, is based on data from the 78th round of the National Sample Survey conducted in 2021. It classifies India’s workforce and learners into five categories: those attending school, going for tertiary education, involved in formal and informal work, women and those not in education, employment and training, or the NEET youth.

“NEET youth are constrained by the absence of income and the sunk cost of prior education,” said the report. “Students often cannot layer paid skilling onto existing financial commitments.”

This group, along with women, needs affordable or subsidised training and financial support, underlined the NITI Aayog. It also said that skilling programmes should be linked to the demand of emerging sectors and self-employment opportunities.

“Across segments, the ability to combine learning with earning remains a central requirement,” it said.

The report further pointed out that only 8.25% of persons who have graduated from college are employed in roles aligned with their qualifications.

“Limited exposure to practical learning and industry-aligned training continues to constrain employability, even among formally educated youth,” it said.

item.title: ‘India’s Forests, Real and Imagined’: Forests as literary-political figures across three millennia
item.description: Alan Johnson’s book complements environmental histories and anthropological studies with a literary-critical focus.
item.content:encoded:
India’s Forests, Real and Imagined: Writing the Modern Nation by Alan Johnson is an ambitious work of literary ecocriticism that attempts to trace the figure of the forest across approximately three millennia of Indian literary history. It looks at the ancient Sanskrit epics and Tamil Sangam poetry, proceeds to colonial-era nationalism and progressive realism, and then to contemporary postcolonial fiction and Indigenous writing.

Ecological realities and fictitious constructs

The book has been published by Bloomsbury Academic as part of a series in environmental humanities and literary studies and is the result of years of research supported by a Fulbright-Nehru award alongside extensive institutional backing from Idaho State University. It is undeniable that the book has had an incredible journey fuelled by evident passion and considerable scholarly range, but there are tensions in a humongous project that aims to accomplish so much within a relatively compact frame.

The introduction of the book invites its readers on an aerial survey of the Indian subcontinent as it might have looked, around 3000 years ago. Johnson moves south from Himalayan Oak Valleys to the forests bearing sal, sandalwood, teak, and neem. item.title: Ramachandra Guha: Historian Sumit Sarkar took his scholarship beyond the confines of the academy
item.description: He was was one of several prabasi Bengali intellectuals who helped make Delhi University the foremost academic institution in all of South Asia.
item.content:encoded:
In a late essay reflecting on his intellectual journey over the decades, Sumit Sarkar remarked: “So far, we Indian historians have written the histories that we wanted to write, following no agenda but our own. That seems to be a fast-vanishing luxury.”

In a long and very productive life, Sarkar – who was born in Calcutta in 1939 and died in Delhi earlier this month – had to confront three historical agendas imposed by others. The first was a dogmatic Marxism which viewed the past through a narrow economistic lens, and was very influential in Sarkar’s hometown (his father, also a historian, was a member of the Communist Party of India).

The second was the interlinked trend of post-modernism and post-colonialism which viewed history as fragmented and culturally relative, and focused on texts and discourses rather than the lived experiences of people in the past.

The third was the religious majoritarianism of the sangh parivar, which glorified Hindus and demonised Muslims, and despite – or perhaps because of – its Manichaeism gained ideological and political ascendancy in the 1990s and beyond.

item.title: 1 in 3 US workers have ‘disposable’ jobs: An economist outlines the public costs
item.description: Their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the costs otherwise associated with lay-offs and fair treatment at work.
item.content:encoded:
When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.

When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.

These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 US workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.

I am a labour economist. In my new book, Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment, I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.

item.title: Can intense interiority in a book leave the reader thoroughly alienated from the narrator’s life?
item.description: ‘I could step into their world for a bit, but I could never really immerse myself.’
item.content:encoded:
This summer I picked up my friend’s half-read copy of Eula Biss’ Having and Being Had and read a hundred pages curled up on his sofa. I did not particularly find it relatable – she is an essayist and educator living in a palatial house in Chicago, and the book is mostly about her own complicated relationship with owning a house and the material reality that emerges from it. But I was hooked.

After that I read Rachel Cusk’s Outline and Annie Ernaux’s Exteriors in quick succession. The books don’t have much in common; they are not all memoirs, and some resemble the literary style of a confessional. But they all wanted me to see the author as someone with a voice, an opinion, a style, a vision. The structural nature of these books reminded me of a conversation with an acquaintance – I could step into their world for a bit, but I could never really immerse myself. Ultimately it was the inevitable solipsism of their world, where there was no respite from their mind – everything existed in the world that solely belonged to them. Solipsistic writing makes interiority a structural necessity, but at the same time leaves you alienated as a reader.

item.title: Supreme Court orders refund of fine paid by Art of Living for Yamuna floodplains damage
item.description: The foundation headed by spiritual leader Sri Sri Ravi Shankar had held an event along the river in March 2016.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Saturday set aside a 2017 National Green Tribunal order that held the Art of Living foundation responsible for damaging the Yamuna floodplains during its three-day event in 2016, Bar and Bench reported. The court also directed the Delhi Development Authority to refund the Rs 5 crore fine that the foundation had paid in 2016 for restoration work.

A bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and NK Singh passed the order on an appeal filed by Vyakti Vikas Kendra India, an organisation associated with the Art of Living Foundation led by spiritual leader Sri Sri Ravi Shankar.

The foundation had held the World Culture Festival in Delhi in March 2016 to mark 35 years since it was founded. Environmentalists and non-governmental organisations had protested against the event being held on the floodplains of the Yamuna, saying that it would irreparably damage the ecologically-sensitive zone.

Before the event was held, a scientific panel of the National Green Tribunal took note of the concerns and recommended a penalty of Rs 120 crore on the Art of Living Foundation. Two days before the event, the tribunal allowed the foundation to go ahead with the celebrations, but fined it Rs 5 crore.

item.title: Army tribunal upholds censure for brigadier over 2023 Poonch civilian deaths
item.description: The custodial deaths took place in the area of responsibility of a battalion operating in a sector commanded by the officer.
item.content:encoded:
The Armed Forces Tribunal on Thursday upheld an administrative censure for a brigadier who was commanding a sector of the Rashtriya Rifles in Jammu and Kashmir’s Poonch district in December 2023 when three civilians died during an interrogation following a militant attack.

The Chandigarh bench of the tribunal rejected retired Brigadier P Acharya’s challenge to the “severe displeasure” award by the Indian Army against him.

The case relates to an incident in 2023. On December 22 that year, a day after a militant attack in Poonch killed four soldiers, Army personnel picked up nine residents of Topa Peer village. Three of the detained civilians – 45-year-old Safeer Ahmad, 26-year-old Mohammad Showkat and 30-year-old Shabir Ahmad – died due to alleged torture in Army custody.

The incident took place in the area of responsibility of 48 Rashtriya Rifles, a battalion operating in a sector commanded by Acharya at the time.

On Thursday, the tribunal found that the officiating commanding officer of 48 Rashtriya Rifles battalion involved in the incident had directed a company commander to use “slightly harsh” methods while interrogating suspects.

item.title: Thinking is a sport, not a chore: Why children’s literature creators will win the war against AI
item.description: A children’s author makes a case for rejecting AI.
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: The following text is entirely human-authored. No “outside” help was sought to outline the piece. Editing was not outsourced to a “foreign hand”. Research was strictly restricted to gossip, Google and good ol’ social media skulking. Synonyms were deployed the old-fashioned way (many thanks, Roget’s International Thesaurus). Sentences were completed unassisted. Deadline was missed by a mile. Slap on that “100% unaided by AI” sticker already.


With that out of the way, let’s get started on the much-dreaded, oft-debated, forever-relevant subject of AI.

My first brush with it? Many, many decades ago. In the presence of a responsible adult. For a short story.

“AIEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE!!!!!” went a particularly excitable character from the aforementioned work of fiction.

item.title: Maharashtra paid Rs 9,605 crore to ineligible beneficiaries under Ladki Bahin scheme: Report
item.description: Though verification drives removed several categories of ineligible recipients, payments had already been made to them, reported the ‘Hindustan Times’.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra government disbursed Rs 9,605 crore to 92 lakh ineligible beneficiaries under its Mukhyamantri Majhi Ladki Bahin Yojana in two years, reported the Hindustan Times citing data obtained through a Right to Information application.

The scheme, launched in June 2024, provides a monthly transfer of Rs 1,500 to women aged 21 to 65 whose families earn less than Rs 2.5 lakh per year.

Though verification drives removed several categories of ineligible recipients, payments had already been made to them, the Hindustan Times reported.

Of the 92 lakh beneficiaries removed by June 2026, sixty-two lakh had failed to complete the e-KYC, or Know Your Customer process, the newspaper reported. In the case of 16 lakh beneficiaries, the Rs 2.5 lakh annual family income limit had been exceeded.

Another 3.6 lakh women were already receiving benefits under the Sanjay Gandhi Niradhar Anudan Yojana, 2.5 lakh were removed because another family member was enrolled, 1.8 lakh were over the age limit of 65 and 4.5 lakh were government employees.

A further 1.7 lakh beneficiaries were excluded after district-level verification, the Hindustan Times reported.

However, more than 2.1 crore women received payments for 17 months till November 2025 and the number of beneficiaries was 2.4 crore between February 2025 and May 2025, the newspaper reported.

item.title: Jharkhand: Protesters clash with police, JMM workers after HC stays recruitment cancellation
item.description: The protesters accused the state government of ‘deceiving’ and ‘betraying’ job aspirants.
item.content:encoded:
Students protesting the Jharkhand High Court’s stay on the cancellation of recruitment appointments tried to burn effigies of Chief Minister Hemant Soren and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi in Ranchi on Friday, leading to clashes with police and Jharkhand Mukti Morcha workers, PTI reported.

The protesters, under the banner of the Jharkhand Public Service Commission-Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission accused the state government of “deceiving” and “betraying” job aspirants.

The Mahagathbandhan alliance, led by Soren’s Jharkhand Mukti Morcha and comprising the Congress, Rashtriya Janata Dal and the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation, is in power in Jharkhand.

On Thursday, the High Court stayed the state government’s decision to cancel the 11th to 13th Jharkhand Public Service Commission Combined Civil Services examinations.

The court also directed candidates selected through the examinations to resume their duties immediately.

Following this, the Jharkhand Public Service Commission-Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission Reforms Manch had called on students to burn effigies of Soren across all 24 districts of Jharkhand, ANI reported.

Tension rose in Ranchi when students moved forward with the effigies and police seized them, the news agency reported.
